source: The mirror equation works for lenses too, and real images form on the far side of the lens.
Students forget that a diverging lens has a negative focal length.

The The Mirror Equation works for thin lenses too, with one change in where things are. For a lens, a real image forms on the far side, where the light goes, so that is where $d_i > 0$. Everything else, including the magnification, carries over from Lenses and Ray Diagrams.

$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}, \qquad m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}.$$ $f > 0$ for a converging lens, $f < 0$ for a diverging lens. $d_i > 0$: real image on the far side. $d_i < 0$: virtual image on the object's side.

The same similar triangles as for a mirror appear. The ray through the center goes straight, so the object and image tips line up through the center: $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}$. The parallel ray bends through $F$, giving $\frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{d_i - f}{f}$. Setting them equal gives the same equation. The geometry is a mirror unfolded.
As the object approaches $F$, the image runs off far away and grows. Inside $F$ it jumps to the object's side as a virtual image.

Forgetting that a diverging lens has a negative focal length. A diverging lens with "$f = 20\ \text{cm}$" means $f = -20\ \text{cm}$ in the equation. Check: a diverging lens alone always gives $d_i < 0$ and $0 < m < 1$.
An object is $7.5\ \text{cm}$ from a converging lens with $f = 5.0\ \text{cm}$. Find $d_i$ and $m$.
$d_i = 15\ \text{cm}$: a real image on the far side.
An object is $30\ \text{cm}$ from a diverging lens with $f = -20\ \text{cm}$.
A projector puts a slide $10.0\ \text{cm}$ from its lens and a sharp image on a screen $4.0\ \text{m}$ away. What focal length does the lens have?
$f = 0.0976\ \text{m} = 9.76\ \text{cm}$. The magnification is $m = -40$, so the slide is turned upside down to come out upright.
Optometrists use the power $P = 1/f$ in diopters (with $f$ in meters): a $+2.5\ \text{D}$ reading lens has $f = 40\ \text{cm}$.
